---
title: "Greedy Exchange: Prove the First Choice Is Safe"
description: "Memorisable mathematical reasoning with small numerical examples."
---

## When to recognise the pattern

When an obvious local choice seems optimal but needs justification.

## The key question

**How do you prove choosing an earliest-ending interval never reduces the maximum number of compatible intervals?**

## Formula worth memorising

$$
f(g)\le f(o)\ \Longrightarrow\ \text{the remaining choices after }g\supseteq\text{those after }o
$$

**Every symbol explained:** g is the greedy interval and o the first interval of an optimal solution; f(x) is an interval's finish time; ≤ means g finishes no later. The subset/superset sign says the set of later intervals compatible with o is also compatible with g, assuming interval selection based on end≤next start.

**Substitute actual numbers:** Suppose available intervals are [1,2], [1,4], [2,3]. Greedy picks [1,2] because it ends at 2. It can then take [2,3], getting 2 intervals. Choosing [1,4] prevents both, giving only 1.

## Why this is mathematically correct

Take an optimal solution with a first interval o. Replace o with greedy earliest-finishing g. Because g ends no later, every later interval of the optimal solution still fits after g. Therefore there exists an equally good optimal solution beginning with g; repeat inductively.

## Limits and counterexamples

If intervals have different rewards, earliest-finish greedy may fail; weighted interval scheduling needs DP. The boundary inequality assumes touching endpoints are compatible (half-open intervals).

## The 20-second memory card

**Memorise: Compare greedy's first choice with an optimal first choice, swap them, and prove no later choice becomes invalid.**

Now reproduce the equation, example and proof aloud, without looking.

**Interview problems:** Non-overlapping Intervals; Maximum Number of Meetings.
